title: Slow-cooker ham in cider
subtitle: Gammon joint cooked gently in apple and cider
excerpt: A whole gammon joint simmered in dry cider with apple, onion, and aromatics until the meat is very tender. Carve and serve warm, or glaze and roast for a golden finish.
sourceNotes: Gammon cooked in cider is a British autumn and winter tradition, common in West Country cooking where cider production is centred. Documented in various British regional cookbooks of the 20th century.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool, slice, and freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the day before, refrigerate in its liquid, and slice cold. The ham keeps in the fridge for up to 5 days.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hind leg of pork that has been cured by salting or brining. It is sold raw and becomes ham once cooked. Gammon joints are typically sold bone-in or boneless.

content.text: in cider rather than water or cola gives the meat a gentle apple sweetness and a more complex broth. The slow cooker is very well suited to gammon: the low heat draws the salt out gradually, the meat stays moist, and by the end of cooking it pulls apart with almost no effort.

The joint can be served straight from the pot, carved at the table. If you want a glazed finish, brush the surface with honey or mustard and put it under a hot grill for 5 to 8 minutes. Both approaches are good; the plain version is simpler and the glazed version is more of a centrepiece.
Serve with mashed potato, roasted root vegetables, or parsley sauce.

Place {{gammon-joint}} of gammon joint in the slow cooker. Surround with {{apple}} quartered apple and {{onion}} halved onion. Add {{bay-leaves}} of bay, {{peppercorns-black}} peppercorns, and {{mustard-powder}} of mustard powder if using. Pour over {{dry-cider}} of dry cider. Add enough cold water so the liquid comes halfway up the joint.

Set the slow cooker to LOW and cook for 6 to 7 hours. The joint is ready when a skewer passes through without resistance and the internal temperature has reached 68°C. Lift it out carefully and rest on a board for 20 minutes before carving.
Score the fat in a diamond pattern, brush with {{honey}} of honey, and grill under high heat for 5 to 8 minutes until the surface is golden and sticky. Watch it closely as the glaze can burn quickly.

rows.cause: Some gammon joints are heavily cured and need soaking before cooking.
rows.fix: Next time, soak the joint in cold water for 2 to 4 hours before cooking to draw out some of the salt. Discard the soaking water.

rows.symptom: The joint is not cooked through after 7 hours
rows.cause: Very large joints or boneless joints rolled tightly may need longer than 7 hours on LOW.
rows.fix: Switch to HIGH for a further hour and check again. A probe thermometer is the best way to check: aim for 68°C at the centre.

rows.symptom: The cooking liquid is very salty and cannot be used as stock
rows.cause: The salt from the gammon has leached into the liquid during cooking.
rows.fix: Taste the liquid before using it. If it is too salty for stock, use it as a cooking liquid for vegetables or discard it. Unsalted gammon produces a usable broth.

rows.symptom: The skin or rind is tough and rubbery
rows.cause: Rind does not soften well in moist slow cooking.
rows.fix: Remove the rind before cooking if it is present. Leave the fat layer underneath; this is what crisps under the grill.

content.text: Ham cooked in cider is a West Country tradition, rooted in the cider-making counties of Somerset, Devon, and Herefordshire where apples and pigs have always gone together. The pairing makes flavour sense: the apple acidity cuts through the fat of the pork and the slight sweetness flatters the cure. It belongs on the table in autumn with something rooted and starchy alongside.
